newsitem.title: UK: British opposition to keep low tax, low spending.
newsitem.headline: British opposition to keep low tax, low spending.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party on Monday put the government on the defensive by committing itself to maintaining the low-tax, low-spending profile of the Conservatives whom it hopes to replace in power within months.

Fighting back, the government poured scorn on claims by Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, that once in power he would tolerate neither higher public spending nor a rise in personal taxation.
"Hell will freeze before Gordon Brown could control spending and keep tax down," finance minister Kenneth Clarke said.
With a general election less than four months away, the Conservative government is trailing by around 20 points in the polls and has lost its overall majority in parliament.

Prime Minister John Major favours a May 1 election, but after the death of a Conservative MP pushed his government into a minority position in parliament last week, there was speculation he might be forced into an earlier poll.
However, on Monday, Labour said one of its MPs, Martin Redmond, has also died, meaning the 322 Conservative MPs are now faced by the same number of legislators from opposition parties.
Pressed at a news conference to say whether Brown's pledge would cut the Conservatives chances of staying in office, Clarke insisted voters would find Labour's commitments incredible.
He denounced Brown as evasive and slippery and said his promises could not be trusted. "Gordon Brown's claim that he could control public spending is beyond belief," he said.
Brown told BBC radio earlier on Monday he would keep both basic rate and the top rate of income unchanged over the five-year life of the next parliament if Labour comes to power.
Britain's 23 percent basic income tax rate and 40 percent top rate are among the lowest in Europe.
There had been speculation that Labour, which has traditionally used tax to create a more equal society, would introduce a 50 percent rate on very high earners.
But Brown will say in a speech : "It is because we understand the importance of work that there will be no return to penal marginal tax rates at the top.
"As a signal of our intentions, I want to make clear that we will not introduce a new top rate of tax."
Instead Brown promises that Labour will introduce, when it is economically feasible, a 10 percent starting rate of income tax to benefit low-income families.
Brown will also accept the tough public spending targets already announced for the next two financial years by Clarke.
"No credible chancellor would do anything other than what I will do, which is to have tough controls on public spending. I have to accept the need for prudence," he said.
And according to media reports, he will say he will maintain a current freeze on pay for government workers despite that fact that Labour is heavily bankrolled by public sector trade unions.
The pledges leave Labour dependent mainly on a "windfall tax" on excess profits of utility companies privatised by the Conservatives for money to devote to cherished objectives.

Brown is now thought to be planning to raise 10 billion pounds ($17 billion) from this one-off tax, using this largely to launch a massive drive to tackle the twin problems of long-term unemployment and jobless school leavers.
He believes this would cut government spending on unemployment benefit and welfare, enabling resources to be rechannelled into areas such as education.
But Clarke said Labour had already made pledges involving some 30 billion pounds ($50 billion) extra government spending.
